opus-5.5.text:
I think my view has shifted quite a bit over the past year or two. There was a period, maybe around 2024, when a lot of people in the field, and I was somewhat in that camp too, felt that pre-training was approaching a wall. The narrative was: we've basically used up the high-quality internet text, scaling compute alone gives diminishing returns, and the real action is going to move to post-training and reinforcement learning. RL was the exciting new frontier, and pre-training felt a bit like a solved, mature engineering problem.

Now I think that was too pessimistic. When you actually work closely on pre-training, you realize how much room there still is. It's not just about throwing more tokens and more FLOPs at the model. There's a lot of headroom in data quality, data mixture, synthetic data, how you handle long context, architecture details, and optimization. Each of these individually might give you a few percent, but they compound. And the base model's capability sets the ceiling for what RL can do afterwards. If the base model is stronger, RL is more efficient and goes further. So in a sense, the progress in RL actually made me appreciate pre-training more, not less.

The other thing is that "pre-training" and "post-training" are becoming less clearly separated. Some things we used to do only in post-training, like reasoning-heavy data or agentic trajectories, can be pushed earlier into mid-training or even pre-training. So when people ask whether pre-training has hit a limit, I think the question itself is a bit outdated. The overall recipe of building a strong foundation still has a lot of scope, and I'd say it's still one of the most important levers we have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pre-training improvements and compounding gains, but does not characterize scaling laws as a framework for identifying which approaches are more effective.

r002.rationale: It does not compare progress at Anthropic or Gemini with stagnation at OpenAI.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say my view has shifted quite a bit, and honestly it's still shifting.

A couple of years ago I would have said pre-training is close to a solved problem in the sense that the recipe is known, and the remaining gains are mostly about scaling compute and data. And I think a lot of people around 2024 started to feel that the curve was flattening. You know, the "data wall" discussion, the sense that we'd basically consumed the high-quality internet, and that the next model wouldn't feel that different from the last one. That was part of why I wrote about the "second half": the first half was about building better priors through pre-training, and the second half is about environments, evaluation, and reinforcement learning on top of those priors.

But I want to be careful, because I think there's a lazy version of that argument, which is "pre-training is done, everything is RL now." I don't believe that. What I believe is that the marginal returns have moved, not disappeared.

Let me try to break it down a bit. There are really three things people lump together under "pre-training."

The first is raw scale: more parameters, more tokens, same recipe. Here I do think the easy gains are mostly taken. Not because scaling laws stopped working, but because the cost of each additional unit of improvement has gotten really steep, and the bottleneck is increasingly data, not compute.

The second is the quality and composition of the data. This is where I've become more optimistic than I was. Synthetic data, data from agents interacting with environments, data that's filtered or rewritten by models themselves. We used to think of pre-training data as something you find on the internet. Now it's something you can partially manufacture, and that changes the shape of the problem. It's less like mining and more like farming.

The third thing, and this is the one I think is underrated, is that pre-training and RL are not really separate stages anymore. The prior you build in pre-training determines what RL can even reach. If the base model has never seen a certain kind of reasoning or tool use, RL has a very hard time discovering it from scratch. So a lot of what looks like "RL progress" is actually pre-training quietly getting better at producing models that are easier to steer. The boundary between the two halves is blurrier than my own essay made it sound.

So if you ask me how much room is left, my honest answer is: in the old sense, maybe not that much. In the new sense, where pre-training is about shaping priors for agents and for RL, I think there's a lot, and we're actually at the beginning of understanding it.

One more thing I've updated on. I used to think of generalization as mostly a property of the pre-trained model. Now I think the more interesting question is generalization across tasks and environments after RL, and that depends heavily on the base. We see models that are very strong on math or code after RL but don't transfer that to, say, long-horizon agentic tasks. Why? I think a big part of the answer is in what the prior looks like. That pulls me back toward pre-training as a research problem, not just an engineering one.

So, less room in the obvious direction, more room in directions we haven't fully named yet. That's roughly where I am now.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become more cautious about saying that pre-training is running out of room. It’s easy to look at the limitations of current models and conclude that the next breakthrough has to come from somewhere else. But a limitation of today’s models isn’t necessarily a limitation of pre-training itself.

I think it helps to separate two questions. One is whether scaling the same recipe on similar data will keep producing the gains we’ve seen before. The other is whether there is still substantial progress available through better data, different objectives, or new kinds of training environments. You can be skeptical about the first and still optimistic about the second.

At the same time, I increasingly think about progress at the level of the whole system. A model can have a lot of knowledge and still struggle to use it reliably over a long task. So there’s room to improve the underlying model, and there’s room to improve how it learns to act, gets feedback, and corrects mistakes. I wouldn’t treat those as competing explanations for where progress will come from.

sol-6.1.text:
I’ve become more cautious about saying that pre-training is running out of room. It’s easy to look at a particular recipe and see diminishing returns, but that doesn’t establish the limit of pre-training itself. The data distribution, the training objective, and how efficiently the model learns can all change.

At the same time, I think we should distinguish better prediction from greater usefulness. A model can gain knowledge through pre-training and still struggle to use that knowledge reliably over a long task. That leaves substantial room for post-training, reasoning, and interaction with an environment.

So I’d frame the question less as “How much pre-training is left?” and more as “Where does the next unit of compute create the most useful capability?” Pre-training remains part of that, but I’m less convinced that scaling it alone is the whole story.
